sections.title: Why Water Science Matters
sections.text: 🌊 Why Water Science Matters Healthy water is the foundation of animal care. ▼ “Healthy water for our animals is as important as healthy air is to you and me.” The Aquarium depends on a continuous supply of clean seawater from Monterey Bay. Water quality affects animal survival, behavior, health, exhibit clarity, and guest experience. Natural seawater connects the exhibits directly to Monterey Bay. Life support systems move, filter, oxygenate, monitor, and return water safely. Maintenance keeps pipes, pumps, filters, valves, and sensors working reliably.

sections.title: Water Source: Monterey Bay
sections.text: 🌊 Water Source: Monterey Bay Natural seawater enters through the intake system. ▼ Seawater is drawn from Monterey Bay and routed through the Aquarium’s life support systems. This gives many exhibits a direct connection to the local marine environment. Monterey Bay → Intake pipe → Pump house → Filtration/Life Support → Exhibits → Overflow/Discharge Volunteer phrase: “The Aquarium is not just displaying the bay; in many ways, it is actively connected to the bay.”

sections.title: Where Does the Water Go?
sections.text: 🔄 Where Does the Water Go? Basic flow path and discharge points. ▼ The Aquarium receives roughly 2,000 gallons per minute of seawater from Monterey Bay. Intake ~2,000 gpm → Kelp Forest ~1,500 gpm + specific exhibits ~200 gpm → Ocean’s Edge/Open Sea/other systems KF: Kelp Forest OE: Ocean’s Edge OS: Open Sea TRCC: Touch/Rocky Coast area ARCC: Animal Research & Care Center

sections.title: Life Support Systems
sections.text: ⚙️ Life Support Systems The hidden systems that keep water safe. ▼ Life support systems are the Aquarium’s behind-the-scenes water infrastructure. They help maintain appropriate clarity, oxygen, temperature, salinity, chemistry, and circulation for different animals and exhibits. Mechanical filtration: removes particles and debris. Biological filtration: supports microbes that help process animal waste. Protein skimming/foam fractionation: removes dissolved organic material. Ozone/UV: may be used in some systems for water clarity and microbial control. Heating/chilling: keeps exhibit water within animal-specific ranges. Sensors and alarms: monitor system performance and water quality.

sections.title: Biofouling: Life Inside the Pipes
sections.text: 🦪 Biofouling: Life Inside the Pipes Natural marine growth can reduce flow. ▼ Top: biofouling inside a seawater pipe. Bottom: orange foam pipeline pigs used for cleaning. Because the Aquarium uses natural seawater, marine organisms can settle and grow inside intake pipes. This is called biofouling . Common growth may include barnacles, mussels, algae, biofilm, hydroids, tube worms, and other organisms. Biofouling narrows pipe diameter and can reduce water flow. Seasonal upwelling can increase nutrients, productivity, and settlement pressure.

sections.title: Pigging: Cleaning the Intake Pipes
sections.text: 🐷 Pigging: Cleaning the Intake Pipes Foam pigs scrub marine growth from pipes. ▼ Pigging means sending a foam or rubber plug, called a pig , through a pipe to scrape away growth and debris. At MBA, pigging helps remove barnacles, mussels, biofilm, and other growth from seawater intake pipes. Pigging is done roughly every six weeks, with more attention during high-growth seasons. The term “pig” comes from pipeline industries that used similar devices to clean pipes. The orange foam pigs are moved by water pressure through the pipe. Guest phrase: “Those orange cylinders are like giant pipe scrubbers. They keep natural seawater moving to the animals.”

sections.title: Seasonal Upwelling Connection
sections.text: ⬆️ Seasonal Upwelling Connection More nutrients can mean more pipe growth. ▼ Spring/Summer winds → cold deep water rises → nutrients increase → plankton increases → settling organisms increase → more biofouling → more pigging attention Upwelling helps make Monterey Bay productive. That same productivity can also mean more organisms available to colonize seawater pipes and infrastructure.

sections.title: Water Chemistry & Monitoring
sections.text: 🔬 Water Chemistry & Monitoring Testing helps catch problems early. ▼ Water teams monitor parameters that affect animal health and system stability. Temperature, salinity, pH, dissolved oxygen, and clarity Ammonia, nitrite, nitrate, alkalinity, and other chemistry markers Flow, pressure, pumps, valves, sensors, and alarms

sections.title: Maintenance & Operations
sections.text: 🛠️ Maintenance & Operations Preventive work keeps systems reliable. ▼ Pigging intake pipes Cleaning filters and strainers Maintaining pumps, valves, sensors, and alarms Checking backup systems and emergency procedures Coordinating with animal care, water quality, and operations teams

sections.title: Discharge Points
sections.text: 📍 Discharge Points Permitted seawater return locations. ▼ SEA-1: Ocean’s Edge tidal basin discharge SEA-2: Ocean’s Edge backflush discharge SEA-3: Sea Otter exhibit overflow discharge SEA-4: Open Sea intertidal discharge

sections.title: Visitor Questions
sections.text: ❓ Visitor Questions Concise floor-ready answers. ▼ Why don’t the pipes clog completely? They are maintained regularly. Pigging scrubs away marine growth before it can seriously restrict flow. Why use natural seawater? Natural Monterey Bay seawater helps recreate local marine conditions and supports exhibits connected to the bay ecosystem. What are the orange cylinders? They are pipeline pigs — large foam scrubbers pushed through pipes by water pressure. Does upwelling affect the Aquarium? Yes. Upwelling increases nutrients and productivity in the bay, which can also increase growth in seawater pipes. Is all water the same for every exhibit? No. Different animals and exhibits may need different temperatures, flow, filtration, lighting, and water quality conditions.

sections.title: Volunteer Talking Points
sections.text: 💬 Volunteer Talking Points Quick language for the floor. ▼ “The Aquarium pumps about 2,000 gallons of seawater every minute.” “The Open Sea exhibit holds about 1.2 million gallons.” “Natural seawater brings a challenge: real marine life grows inside the pipes.” “Pigging is like sending a giant scrubber through a pipe.” “Healthy water is as important to these animals as healthy air is to us.”
